caption: Figure 6.0.1: Behind the curtain of modern LLMs lies a story of scale: billions of parameters trained on trillions of tokens, governed by mathematical scaling laws that predict performance before a single GPU is fired up.
Figure 6.1.1: Unlike humans who read left to right, BERT reads both ways at once. It is the only reader that starts a book from both covers simultaneously.
Figure 6.2.2: Span corruption turns your training text into Swiss cheese: random chunks get removed, and the model learns to fill the holes.
Figure 6.3.2: The power law in action: straight lines on a log-log plot that predict model performance with remarkable accuracy.
Figure 6.3.3: Chinchilla versus Kaplan: two different recipes for spending your compute budget, with very different conclusions about how much data you actually need.
Figure 6.5.1: Adam: the GPS navigator of optimizers, maintaining separate learning rates for each parameter so no gradient gets left behind.
Figure 6.5.2: Learning rate warmup: you would not sprint at full speed the moment you wake up, and neither should your optimizer.
Figure 6.6.3: Mixed precision training is like strategic suitcase packing: use smaller formats where precision is less critical, saving space for what matters.
Figure 6.7.1: In-context learning is the ultimate open-book exam: give the model a few examples in the prompt and watch it figure out the pattern.
Figure 6.7.2: Mesa-optimization is the Russian nesting doll of AI: an optimizer inside your optimizer, learning its own objectives during training.

Figure 7.0.1: The LLM ecosystem as a bustling marketplace: closed-source frontier models push capability boundaries while open-weight releases democratize access, and a new class of reasoning models reshapes what is possible.
Figure 7.1.1: The frontier model race: OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google sprint to build ever more capable systems while the rest of us try to keep up.
Figure 7.3.1: Reasoning models think before they speak, generating internal chains of thought that (usually) lead to better answers.
Figure 7.4.1: Multilingual models juggle dozens of languages at once, occasionally mixing them up like a polyglot at a very international dinner party.
Figure 8.1.1: Reasoning models allocate more thinking time to harder problems, just as skilled players deliberate longer on critical moves.

Figure 8.2.1: The reasoning model landscape as an archipelago: each island represents a model family (o1/o3, DeepSeek R1, QwQ), with bridges showing shared training techniques and architectural patterns.
Figure 8.3.1: RLVR as a training gym: the model gets stronger at reasoning by practicing on verifiable problems, with automatic scoring replacing the need for human judges.

Figure 8.4.1: Reasoning models prefer simple, direct prompts. Elaborate chain-of-thought scaffolding (left) can interfere with the model's trained reasoning process, while a clear problem statement (right) lets it think freely.
Figure 8.5.1: Compute-optimal inference means matching the reasoning budget to problem difficulty: easy questions need minimal tokens, while hard problems justify the full thinking budget.
Figure 8.6.1: LLMs and formal proof assistants complement each other: the LLM generates proof candidates (creative intuition), while the proof checker verifies every step with mathematical certainty.
Figure 9.0.1: Squeezing every last drop of speed from a giant model is part science, part art. Quantization, caching, and batching are the tools of the trade.
Figure 9.1.1: Quantization puts your model on a strict diet: fewer bits per weight, smaller memory footprint, and surprisingly little loss of intelligence.
Figure 9.2.1: The KV cache grows with every token generated; managing it efficiently is the key to high-throughput serving.
Figure 9.3.1: Speculative decoding: a fast junior model drafts tokens and a powerful senior model checks them in bulk, turning serial generation into parallel verification.
Figure 9.4.1: The serving stack is a restaurant kitchen: the load balancer seats guests, the inference engine cooks, and the API layer serves the dishes.
Figure 10.0.1: Think of an LLM API as a hotel concierge: you describe what you need, hand over your key, and the magic happens behind the desk.
Figure 10.1.1: The LLM API marketplace: a bazaar of providers, each with unique strengths, pricing models, and just enough differences to keep your adapter code interesting.
Figure 10.1.2: Think of an LLM API as a hotel receptionist: you describe what you need, they route your request to the right room, and hand back the result.
Figure 10.1.3: Streaming via SSE: tokens arrive on a conveyor belt one by one, so your users see results forming in real time instead of staring at a spinner.
Figure 10.2.1: Structured output is like pouring liquid model output into a JSON-shaped mold: you get exactly the shape you asked for, every time.
Figure 10.2.2: Tool use turns your LLM into a Swiss army knife: it can call functions, query databases, and use APIs instead of just generating text.
Figure 10.3.1: Rate limits are the bouncers of API land: exceed your quota and you will be waiting in line no matter how important your request thinks it is.
Figure 10.3.2: Semantic caching: if someone already asked nearly the same question, why pay to answer it again? Your API bill will shrink accordingly.
Figure 10.3.3: Exponential backoff: each retry waits longer than the last, like a polite guest who knocks less frequently when nobody answers the door.
Figure 10.3.4: The circuit breaker pattern: when an API starts failing, stop hammering it and give it time to recover. Your retry budget will thank you.
Figure 10.4.1: Reasoning models take a moment to think (sometimes quite a long moment) before answering, trading speed for significantly better accuracy.
Figure 10.4.2: Multimodal APIs give your model eyes, ears, and reading glasses all at once, processing images, audio, and text in a single call.
Figure 11.0.1: The same model can be brilliant or baffling depending on how you ask. Prompt engineering is the art of asking the right way.
Figure 11.1.1: Prompt templates are the Mad Libs of AI: fill in the blanks with your specific task, and the model completes the story.
Figure 11.2.1: Tree-of-Thought: instead of one linear chain, the model explores multiple reasoning branches and picks the most promising path.
Figure 11.2.2: Chain-of-thought prompting: making the model show its work, just like your math teacher always insisted you do.
Figure 11.2.3: Self-consistency assembles a jury of model outputs and lets them vote. The majority answer is usually the most reliable one.
Figure 11.3.1: The reflection loop: generate, critique, refine, repeat. The model becomes its own editor, catching mistakes humans might miss.
Figure 11.3.2: Meta-prompting: prompts that write prompts. It is prompts all the way down, and surprisingly, it works.
Figure 11.3.3: Prompt chaining is a relay race: each step processes its piece and hands the baton to the next, building toward the final answer.
Figure 11.4.1: Prompt injection is the Trojan horse of LLM applications: malicious instructions hiding inside innocent-looking user input.
Figure 11.4.2: Defending against prompt injection requires layered defenses. No single wall stops every attack, but multiple barriers make infiltration far harder.
Figure 12.0.1: Not every problem needs a billion parameters. Sometimes the smartest architecture pairs a lightweight ML model with an LLM, each doing what it does best.
Figure 12.1.1: Classical ML and LLMs are different tools in the same toolbox. A screwdriver is not better than a hammer; it depends on whether you have screws or nails.
Figure 12.3.1: The hybrid pipeline assembly line: classical ML handles the fast, predictable parts while the LLM tackles the nuanced, open-ended work.
Figure 12.4.1: The latency-cost-quality trilemma: pick any two and the third one suffers. Hybrid architectures help you cheat by using each approach where it excels.
Figure 12.4.2: The Pareto frontier for a classification task. The hybrid router (orange) achieves near-GPT-4o quality at a fraction of the cost by routing easy queries to cheaper models.
